meta.purpose: Everything on this site that a reviewer should look at before trusting it. Grouped by severity, not by topic. Each row names what was expected, what was found, and where to check it.

severity_key.high: Affects whether the site can earn at all, or whether a claim on the site is currently wrong.
severity_key.medium: Affects usefulness or discoverability, not correctness.
severity_key.low: Cosmetic, administrative, or already resolved with a note.

flags.title: Every submitted path code is 9 characters; every ASIN observed on arrival is 10
flags.expected: An Amazon Standard Identification Number is a 10-character alphanumeric identifier.
flags.found: All five submitted codes (B04G1MEwY, B02NbDxp3, B00hJ57DV, B0c8moW59, B0f3GKalj) are 9 characters and contain lowercase letters. All five destinations now resolve, and they carry 10-character uppercase ASINs: B0CDY277D3, B09B7SB46R, B08DKYBTPH, B0DHZTCNR5 and B0DZFD6R9Z.
flags.impact: The intended_asin field is null for all five rather than filled with the slug. Filling it with the slug would have been an inference.
flags.reading: The submitted codes are short-link slugs rather than identifiers. The register records what arrived, and keeps the two fields separate.
flags.blocks: nothing — but it explains why one column is empty
to_check: Open each supplied link and compare the /dp/ segment to the code in the link

flags.title: Attribution to shopnow047c-20 is not confirmed by an Associates report
flags.expected: A click from this site appears in the Associates report against the supplied tag.
flags.found: The tag was not observed in any URL reached while following the supplied links, and no Associates report has been read. An earlier build appended ?tag=shopnow047c-20 to every Amazon destination anyway; that was withdrawn on 2026-11-20 because a tag invented from a public observation looks like attribution while remaining unconfirmed. The five products now publish as untagged listing links, marked sponsored.
flags.impact: The site earns nothing from those clicks and says so in the footer of every page. Adding a tag is a data change, not a code change: one approved intent record per product, and the build tags that product automatically.
flags.reading: Two separate questions were being confused: does the destination carry a tag, and does the account register a click. The first is not met yet, because the published links carry no tag. The second needs a click and a dashboard.
flags.blocks: any claim that the site can currently earn
to_check: One click from the owner's device, then Reports → Orders in the Associates dashboard

flags.found: The links are of the form link.amazon/<code>. This build could not establish from an official source whether that is an Amazon-issued redirect that applies a tag server-side, or an untagged redirect.
flags.impact: The site does not use the short links as click destinations any more; it links to the resolved listing with the tag attached. The short link stays in the record as evidence of what was supplied.
flags.reading: Unresolved is not invalid. Nothing on the site calls these links invalid or non-compliant.

flags.title: The only supported route to price and availability data is gated behind 10 qualifying sales
flags.expected: A site can decide to add prices once it has a data feed.
flags.found: Program Policies §2(b) still names “Creators API or PA API” as the permitted route. Amazon's own documentation now records PA-API 5 as deprecated and returning 403 AccessDeniedException, and lists the Creators API prerequisites as Associates enrolment, at least 10 qualifying sales within the past 30 days, registration through Associates Central, and generated credentials.
flags.reading: This turns the site's biggest missing feature into a sequencing problem rather than an engineering one. Prices arrive after the site proves it can sell, not before. A separate clause in the same section adds that a comparison-format price display must also show the lowest used price, which is a second reason this site's comparison table keeps its price column empty.
flags.impact: The comparison table keeps its blank price column by rule, and the site's own price_rule wording was updated to name the deprecation rather than pointing at an API that no longer answers.
flags.blocks: any live price, rating or availability display, until the sales threshold is met

flags.title: Open reading: may plain listing links stay untagged before a Special Link is validated?
flags.expected: A written answer from Amazon Associates on whether untagged listing links are permitted on an enrolled site with no validated Special Link yet.
flags.found: Program Policies 2(b) says 'you must include your Associates ID or tag ... as a parameter in the URL of each link you place on your Site to an Amazon Site'. The same section opens 'General Requirements Applicable to All Special Links'. Reading A (this build): the tag rule governs Special Links, so a plain listing link is not one. Reading B (an earlier session's reading, FLG-009 history): every link to an Amazon site must carry the ID.
flags.reading: Reading A is the more literal one given the section heading. It is still an interpretation, and the cost of being wrong is a policy breach, so it needs the owner's decision in the enrolled workflow.

flags.title: The repository's robots.txt sits in a subdirectory of the host, which crawlers are not required to read
flags.expected: A robots.txt that crawlers consult before indexing the site.
flags.found: Google's robots specification states that robots.txt must be placed in the top-level directory of a site and that crawlers don't check for robots.txt files in subdirectories. This site is served from https://karagemop466-tech.github.io/Affil1/, so its robots.txt publishes at /Affil1/robots.txt — a subdirectory — and Google may never fetch it. The file itself is correctly formatted (re-checked against the specification on 2026-11-20) and excludes /archive/, but its reach cannot be guaranteed from inside a project repository.
flags.reading: Discovery does not depend on it: every generated page carries a self-referencing canonical URL, the sitemap lists only the maintained edition, and internal links are relative and resolved. The step that actually puts the sitemap in front of Google is Search Console submission, which needs the owner's account (Q-11, S-03).
flags.impact: Discoverability, not correctness. The file is kept correctly formatted for any crawler that does read it; canonicals and the sitemap carry the load if it is ignored.
flags.blocks: nothing — but Search Console submission (Q-11 / S-03) is the required discovery step, not an optional one

flags.title: Two CI steps reported green while testing the wrong directory, and the collector could not import
flags.expected: The gates that stand in front of a deploy run this repository's own tests, and any step that collects nothing is a failure.
flags.found: Three defects, each reproduced on main at 2934ed0 on 2026-11-20. (1) edition-verify.yml ran 'python3 -m unittest discover -s platform'; the directory has been _platform since the Pages rename, so unittest imported CPython's stdlib platform package and printed 'Ran 45 tests' from test.test_support while running none of the platform suite. (2) kitchen-check.yml ran only 'py_compile' over _analytics/endpoint.py, which does not import at all: it inserts ROOT/'tools' on sys.path and then 'from build import GENERATED', so the module and its test suite both raised ModuleNotFoundError. (3) _tools/arm_links.py reads _src/_data/product-intent.json, which does not exist, so the owner's arming switch died with FileNotFoundError on --status before printing any state.
flags.impact: Any release receipt on this board that cites the 'platform unit & HTTP collector tests' step as evidence was citing a step that did not test the platform. Repaired on branch arena/3e17592d-affil1: both steps now target _platform and _analytics, each fails when discovery collects nothing (negative-tested against an empty directory and against the singular 'Ran 1 test' line), and the collector's suite passes. No product observation, confirmation or revenue figure changed.
flags.reading: A check that passes on code it never imported is worse than no check, because it gets quoted afterwards as verification. The general rule for the next session: if a command can succeed while collecting zero tests, it is not a gate.
flags.blocks: nothing — repaired here, recorded so earlier receipts can be re-read
to_check: python3 -m unittest discover -s _platform -p 'test_*.py' (6 tests) versus -s platform (45 stdlib tests)

flags.title: Reader-facing pages asserted a tracking tag that the paid-link gate had withheld
flags.expected: A page may not imply that a purchase can be credited to an Associates account while the intent register records no confirmation, and the disclosure has to stay true in both gate states.
flags.found: All 10 published guides carried a sidebar sentence reading 'Product links in these guides earn a commission. They are marked sponsored and every one carries the site's Amazon tag', and every product page's fine print read 'Paid link · … · tag shopnow047c-20'. The hrefs on those same pages are plain https://www.amazon.com/dp/ listing links with no tag parameter (0 tagged hrefs in the generated tree, measured 2026-11-20), and _src/data/product-intent.json records associate_enrollment_confirmed, site_registered and one_link_test_completed as null. The rel='sponsored' marking claim was true; the attribution claim was not.
flags.impact: The guide wording and the product fine print now follow the URL that is actually on the page: an untagged permitted link reads 'Listing source · … · this link carries no tracking tag, so nothing here can be credited to an account yet', and the tagged wording becomes available the moment arm_links.py records an approved Special Link. The annex's disclosure line, which printed the tracking ID as though it were applied, was amended in the same pass. The verbatim Associates sentence is untouched on every page.
flags.reading: Wording that describes a gate state rather than the current state is a defect that reads like confidence. It was rewritten to be conditional in both directions, not deleted, because the disclosure obligation does not depend on the gate.
flags.blocks: nothing — wording corrected on this branch
to_check: python3 _tools/arm_links.py --status (now runs; prints 'published state: reference links only')

flags.title: The host was publishing two branded publications of the same five listings, both indexable
flags.expected: One site for a search engine to index, with one sitemap, one feed and one set of canonical URLs.
flags.found: The generated shop at the repository root (Crisp & Counter, 34 pages) and the Countertop Almanac edition under /edition/ (27 pages) describe the same five listings under different mastheads, each with self-referencing canonical URLs, its own sitemap.xml, its own feed.xml and its own RSS autodiscovery link; the annex also advertised its own sitemap in edition/robots.txt. No crawler rule could have resolved it: a robots.txt file must sit at the root of the host and cannot be placed in a subdirectory, so neither /Affil1/robots.txt nor /Affil1/edition/robots.txt is read at all (see FLG-027), and robots.txt is explicitly not a mechanism for keeping a page out of Google.
flags.impact: All 27 annex pages now emit <meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">, carry a visible 'This is the verification annex' note linking to the shop, and no longer advertise a second sitemap. verify_edition.py asserts the tag, the note and the robots file on every page (2,047 line-by-line checks, up from 1,965) and was negative-tested by stripping the tag and the note from one page. The shop's sitemap was already correct and is unchanged. Open half: whether the annex is eventually folded into the shop's tables or retired (Q-16).
flags.reading: Deleting another session's edition would have destroyed reviewable work; pointing a search engine at one of the two is the smaller, reversible act. 'follow' is deliberate: a blocked crawl cannot read the tag that does the work.
flags.blocks: nothing — the annex stays reachable for review

flags.title: Three first-party collectors exist, and one of them can never match the published site
flags.expected: One collector with a page allowlist that matches the URLs the site actually publishes.
flags.found: _analytics/endpoint.py (imports the build's GENERATED set; broken until this branch, now importing and passing its suite), _measurement/collector.py (reads src/data/product-intent.json, a path that no longer exists, so its approved-link allowlist always resolves to empty, and it validates page names 'probe', 'flagged' and 'desk' from an older URL scheme that the shop does not use) and _platform/collector.py (the annex's own). Nothing in the published pages can be measured by more than one of them, and only the first is exercised by CI.

The practical consequence today is nil, because no collector is enabled - the client stays inert until CC_ANALYTICS_ENABLED is set by a host that does not exist yet.

flags.blocks: Q-25 (which collector is canonical) blocks any real measurement rollout
